extracted.subtask_description: A worksheet to guide 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter-eligibility (SME) analysis for claims potentially directed to abstract ideas, following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance (Steps 1, 2A, 2B). Intended to be completed per-claim in examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and establish BRI (Section I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a separate worksheet for each claim. Identify what applicant invented (summary sentence(s) of the invention) and then state the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim limitations (e.g., recited components and their functions). Suggested to use the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance Quick Reference Sheet and flowchart when performing this step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter) (Step 1)? Choose A or B:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A (yes), continue SME analysis. If B (no), make a rejection under non‑statutory subject matter using Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01. If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and consider suggesting a potential amendment; make the assumption clear in the record if a Step 2 rejection is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found certain concepts to be 'abstract ideas', for example fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves (standing alone), or mathematical relationships/formulae. A claim is 'directed' to an abstract idea when the abstract idea is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A, B, or C: A) No — claim does not recite a concept similar to those found abstract (conclude SME analysis). B) Yes, but streamlined analysis appropriate (eligibility is self-evident; full analysis not needed). C) Yes — identify the claim limitation(s) that correspond to the abstract idea and explain why the recited subject matter is an abstract idea. When identifying similarity, refer to examples previously held abstract by courts (e.g., intermediate settlement in Alice, risk hedging in Bilski, tax-free investing in Fort Properties). If claiming 'directed to an abstract idea', continue to Step 2B unless streamlined analysis applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes, but the streamlined analysis is appropriate as the eligibility is self-evident, and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply streamlined analysis (refer to February 2015 Training Slides) when the claimed invention is not focused on the abstract idea and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up the abstract idea such that others cannot practice it. If applicable, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional claim elements beyond the abstract idea (Step 2B presence check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the abstract idea identified above? Choose 1 or 2:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) No — if there are no additional elements beyond the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection and continue with other patentability requirements (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015). Also consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to make the claim eligible and identify them for applicant. 2) Yes — list the specific additional elements (e.g., memory, processor programmed to perform steps, network interface, controller, electronic funds transfer, kiosk with interactive display, smart card dispenser) and continue to evaluate their significance under Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the significance of additional elements (search for an inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying additional elements and evaluating their significance involves the search for an 'inventive concept' in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea. Reasons supporting significance may include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the abstract idea with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions; not merely adding 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending well-understood, routine, and conventional activities specified at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not adding insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the abstract idea to a particular technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components / conventional implementation are insufficient (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic computer components recited as performing generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional amount to no more than implementing the abstract idea with a computerized system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are recited at a high level of generality (e.g., 'memory,' 'processor,' 'network interface,' 'electronic funds transfer') and amount to conventional computer implementation or merely transmitting information through unspecified interfaces, they do not impose meaningful limits and therefore do not make the claim 'significantly more' than the abstract idea. Similarly, adding instructions to 'apply' an abstract idea or appending routine data-gathering do not provide the inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude SME analysis and procedural actions (Step 2B conclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any elements, individually or in combination, amount to 'significantly more' than the abstract idea, conclude SME analysis and continue examination under other patentability requirements. If not, conclude SME analysis by making a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When concluding, explain in the record why the claim does or does not amount to significantly more (provide reasoning: which element(s) provide significantly more and how). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 when making rejections. If the claim could be amended to add eligible elements, identify those elements and consider suggesting them to applicant. Clarify the record with remarks in the Office action where helpful (for example: 'the claim recites the abstract idea of X, but amounts to significantly more because Y').
